title: Land ethic

definition.text: A framework for how, ethically, people should regard the land.

facts.text: Aldo Leopold coined the term in A Sand County Almanac (1949), calling for an ethic covering humans' relation to land, animals and plants.
His basic principle: a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability and beauty of the biotic community.
It makes humans plain members and citizens of the land community rather than its conquerors.
Leopold saw two flaws in a land ethic based on economic self-interest: most members of an ecosystem have no economic worth, and conservation gets left to government.
Other land ethics rest on economics, utilitarianism, libertarianism, egalitarianism or ecology.
It is popular as a moderate view that balances human interests with a healthy, diverse natural environment.
Critics say it is vague and does not clearly explain why it should be adopted.

contested_note: Scholars debate what Leopold's land ethic asserts and whether it rests on human interests or the intrinsic value of nature.

definition.text: Land ethics that judge land use by the greatest good for people, or by individual property rights and freedom.

facts.text: Utilitarianism underpins industrial farming, which is defended for raising yields and lowering food prices.
Unlike a purely economic ethic, it can limit a farmer's profit if soil runoff damages neighbours' property.
Garrett Hardin argued in 1968 that the only solution to the tragedy of the commons was to give soil and water to private citizens.
Egalitarian land ethics arose in response, favouring equal access to land or food.

definition.text: Preferences in which a person prefers any amount of one good to any amount of another, looking at the second good only to break ties.

facts.text: The name comes from dictionary ordering, which attends to the first letter and only looks at the next letter in case of ties.
They are the classic example of rational preferences that cannot be represented by any utility function.
They are not continuous, which is why no real-valued utility function can capture them.
If everyone shares the same lexicographic preferences, ordinary general equilibrium cannot exist, because no one would sell.
Clive Spash used them to study ethically motivated refusals to trade species and ecosystems for money.
